chapter_theme: On the minister's counsel and the narrator's word that fate has ripened, the king gives Padumai, whom Civakan cured of snakebite, to Civakan; after the wedding rites and two months of love, which also bring him to Tesikappavai in the grove, he slips from his sleeping wife at night, and she wakes to search for him like a body for its life and to scold her parrot.

cast.role: the hero, called குமரன், வேலான், குருசில் in this chapter
the Pallava king's daughter, cured of snakebite by Civakan and married to him
the king of the city, Padumai's father
the king's minister, who counsels the marriage
the women who perform the wedding rites
the women who bathe and dress the bridegroom
the elders who perform the marriage
a young woman of the grove whom Civakan meets and joins

1340.reading: The king says that, having heard the faultless counsel of his minister Mathidharan, he too sees it clearly: the young man matches her in looks and form, the thing has come as destiny brings it, and the right act is to give his jewelled daughter to the man of the burning spear.
1340.event: The king, after hearing Mathidharan's counsel, decides to give his daughter to Civakan.

claims.claim: a match that destiny has brought, shown by likeness of looks and form, should be fulfilled

1340.nuance: The speaker is named only by the frame (he heard what Mathidharan said and answers with என்றான்); the narrator endorses his reading of fate two verses on, where the portion (பான்மை) is said to have ripened for the spearman (1342).

1341.reading: The king sends the minister to lay all this out plainly; the minister goes and tells it, the prince agrees that it be as the spear-bearing king wishes, and the minister returns to report that the matter is settled.
1341.event: Mathidharan carries the offer to Civakan, who accepts, and reports the acceptance to the king.

1342.reading: The narrator gives the grounds: he brought back her departed life, set flowers in her hair, touched her body and saved her, and is surpassing in beauty; women who have been joined to a man belong to the one who touched them, and so the portion fated for the victorious spearman had ripened.

claims.claim: a woman whose body a man has touched belongs to that man
what is apportioned by fate ripens and comes to the one it is due to

1342.nuance: The touch was the physician's: in 1294 he strokes her whole body to keep her life in. The maxim at line 3 turns that healing touch into a claim on her, so the cure itself becomes the betrothal; the reading of ஒன்றிய and உற்றவர் as touching is the plainest sense of the line, but it is a compressed saying.

1343.reading: The great queen and the victorious king, weighing these things, order that the girl be given that very day to the one bound to her, and the palace is newly dressed with hanging pearl garlands and flowers strewn everywhere.
1343.event: The queen and king order the wedding for that day, and the palace is decorated.

1344.reading: On the day the astrologer fixed, inside the chosen palace, jewelled women recite the auspicious forms, tie the protective cord on the bride's wrist above her lotus hand, and stand round her in worship and guard.
1344.event: On the fixed day the women tie the protective cord on Padumai's wrist.

1345.reading: Women like jewelled dolls bathe the handsome bridegroom with water from a gem pot brought on a young elephant's neck and dress him in the attire fit for the wedding, so that he seems worthy of worship; the bride, a gem-like creeper, looks like a maiden of the gods.
1345.event: Civakan is bathed and dressed for the wedding, and Padumai is adorned.

1346.reading: Elders of a dignity hard to praise perform the marriage of the carp-eyed bride and the Kama-like groom, and the two, free of confusion and of a love native to them, are joined.
1346.event: Elders perform the marriage of Padumai and Civakan.
1346.nuance: இயற்கை அன்பு, a love by nature, presents the match as more than the king's arrangement, in line with the fate of 1340 and 1342.

1347.reading: The bride whose eyes have fought sword and spear and the warrior with the long anklet join shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot as if one form, and day after day share pleasure like the Nagas of the upper world.
1347.event: Padumai and Civakan begin their married life together.

1348.reading: Her hot breasts press against his garland until its buds open and it is crushed, and the poet asks what her pride can now do against such force.
1348.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are compressed and the sense of தணிக்கும் தாமரையாள் நலம் and பிணிக்கும் பீடு is hard to fix; the reading follows line 3 and 4, where the crushing of the garland is plain.

1349.reading: The signs of their love-play: garlands torn, saffron smeared, wreaths wilted, girdles snapped and the anklets sounding as the two, like bees parted from their kin, sport.

1350.reading: On a bed thick with the smoke of rich agil, morning and evening, the two whose love has come joined through seven births go on embracing without tiring.
1350.nuance: எழுமையும் இயைந்து: the narrator treats the love as a bond carried over seven births, a phrase that will sit hard with the hero's departure ten verses on.

1351.reading: Smelling and tasting, listening to the music of strings and watching cool dances, and pressed by her hot breasts, the spearman spends each day, they say.
1351.nuance: The verse runs through the senses one by one, smell, taste, hearing, sight and touch, as the means of his pleasure; என்பவே marks it as report.

1352.reading: The spearman with the gold garland and the smoke-tipped lance falls upon her breasts, where pearl strings shine as if a master had gathered the moon's rays and the many stars and strung them.

1353.reading: A voice praises her: I have seen my life, a creeper of a girl with breasts only this much grown, who lisps a sweet word or two as though afraid her sharp teeth might split it, her long eyes shaming a spear, her body a ghee-dipped sprout.
1353.nuance: The speaker is not named. என் உயிரை யான் கண்டேன் fits the lover beholding his beloved, and the verse is read as Civakan's; but ஒருநாட்காறும் and the stress on how small she still is could belong to a nurse or mother recalling her growth, and the sense of line 3 is uncertain.

1354.reading: Embracing the lightning-waisted, peacock-gentle girl so that her two brows rise and her waist bends, the man of the flower-fresh chest drinks her beauty and crowns her with a honey-dripping garland.
1354.event: Civakan embraces Padumai and puts a garland on her hair.

1355.reading: In the grove where she stays, a young woman with a honey-filled garland and spear-like eyes plays the vina to relieve her loneliness.
1355.event: A young woman plays the vina alone in the grove.
1355.nuance: The woman is not named here. Since in the next verse Civakan enters the grove and meets the one called Tesikappavai, and 1358 speaks of two women, she is read as Tesikappavai rather than Padumai; the garland of line 1 could instead link her to 1354.

1356.reading: The prince enters the grove where tender leaves crowd, flowers abound and bees sleep, and comes face to face with the peacock-like woman called Tesikappavai, whose swaying waist outdoes the lightning of the rain cloud.
1356.event: Civakan enters the grove and meets Tesikappavai.
1356.nuance: Whether தேசிகப் பாவை is a proper name or an epithet of beauty is not certain from this verse; என்னும் suggests a name, and 1358's two women support a second woman.

1357.reading: With her anklets like humming bees and her girdle like sounding bees, the flower-creeper trembles in shame as he joins her and crowns her with a garland of love according to the art; her loneliness gone, her softness puts out a new sprout.
1357.event: Civakan unites with Tesikappavai in the grove.
1357.nuance: கலையினது இயல்பின் says the union follows the rule of an art, the poem's sign that love is treated as a learned discipline as well as a feeling.

1358.reading: To these two women, the one with sandal-bathed breasts and flower bangles, lovely as the lady of the lotus pool, and the one with spear eyes red as if with kings' blood, who daily bow and praise his feet, he is like Ananga.

1359.reading: When two months had passed thus, the spearman put aside the pleasure of her breasts and the love in which they had joined; with his heart risen he set out into the darkness, and the fortune of his settled destiny stood as his chariot.
1359.event: After two months Civakan leaves Padumai and goes out into the night.
1359.nuance: பொறி, fortune or destiny, is made his vehicle: the departure is his own resolve (எழுந்தது உள்ளம்) and his fate at once.

1360.reading: Gently, so that she is not hurt, he takes away his soft arm from where it lay across her garlanded body and goes out into the darkness of the night that has stopped all movement, as a good life goes when it leaves the body.
1360.event: Civakan slips his arm from Padumai while she sleeps and leaves in the dark.

1361.reading: When he left the dark-haired, bangled girl in her sleep, she woke behind him with her spear-like eyes, they say.
1361.event: Padumai wakes after Civakan has gone.

1362.reading: She is like a body that searches for the life that has left it and faints, and like a bird with flower eyes that searches its nest to find its mate.
1362.event: Padumai searches the bed for Civakan.
1362.nuance: The simile reverses the one in 1360: there he went as life leaves the body; here she is the body left behind, which in this image still feels and seeks.

1363.reading: She reproaches the strong young man who, even when they embraced, would say 'it hurts if the jewel presses', and turns in anger on her fine green parrot too: you did not tell me he was leaving the house.
1363.event: Padumai rails at the absent Civakan and scolds her parrot for not warning her.
1363.nuance: The tenderness she remembers (he feared even a jewel between them would hurt her) is turned into the charge against him: one so careful of her body left without a word.

links.note: In 1296 the onlookers say that he alone restored her remaining life and that the king will give the girl to the spearman; here the king, on his minister's counsel, decides exactly that.
links.teaches: The marriage is first the crowd's verdict on the cure and only then the king's decision, so royal policy here ratifies a public judgment that the healer has earned the bride.

links.note: In 1294 Civakan strokes her whole body as a cure, thinking her life will stay if she is seen, spoken to and touched; here the narrator cites that touch, with the maxim that a woman belongs to the one who touched her, as the ground of the marriage.
links.teaches: Read together, the physician's touch made to save a life becomes after the fact a claim on the woman, showing how the epic fuses healing and betrothal into one act of fate.

links.note: The patikam says he delighted in her for two months and then took the road again; this verse gives the two months, the night departure, and his destiny as the chariot that carries him.
links.teaches: The patikam reports only the length of the stay, while the narrative adds that the leaving is driven both by the hero's own rising heart and by fortune, which the summary line never says.

links.note: In 1340 the king reads the match as having come by destiny; in 1359 the hero's destiny (பொறி) is the chariot that takes him away from the same bride after two months.
links.teaches: The same fate that the king cites to make the marriage is what carries the husband off, so in this epic destiny grants a union without promising that it will last.

links.note: The couplet says all five senses find their objects in one bright-bangled woman; the epic names the same five, smell, taste, music, the sight of dance and her touch, as the round of the hero's pleasure.
links.teaches: Where the couplet gathers all five senses into one woman, the epic spreads them over perfumes, food, string music and dance with only touch left to her, showing a prince's pleasure as a court of arts rather than the single person the couplet praises.

gains.a: the verse's list of senses is recognised as the Kural's fivefold scheme of the lover's delight, not a random catalogue
gains.b: the couplet's claim of concentration is set against a scene where the senses are served by many things, which shows how strong its claim that one woman suffices really is

links.note: The couplet says the bond between the lover and the girl is that between body and life; the epic has the husband leave his sleeping wife as a good life leaves the body.
links.teaches: The couplet's simile is a promise that the two cannot part; the epic takes the same simile literally, so the husband's going is a death for the wife, which is the cost the couplet's image leaves unstated.

gains.a: the departure simile is read as the turning of a known love image, the lovers as body and life, into a picture of loss
gains.b: the couplet's image is shown to cut both ways: if he is her life, his leaving makes her a lifeless body

links.note: The couplet likens the bond of body and life to a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; the epic has the abandoned wife as a body searching for its departed life and as a bird searching the nest for its mate.
links.teaches: In the couplet the forsaken body is an empty shell that feels nothing, which is its lesson on impermanence; the epic gives the left-behind body and nest a longing of their own, turning the image of death's indifference into one of grief.

gains.a: the double simile is seen to rework the Kural's figure of body, life, bird and nest, so its pathos rests on a known image of death
gains.b: the couplet's bare picture of the life leaving gains a view from the side of what is left, which the couplet passes over

links.note: In the Kuruntokai poem the woman prays that even when this life turns into the next he may be her husband; the epic's narrator calls the couple's love one joined through seven births.
links.teaches: What the akam speaker can only pray for, the epic narrator states as fact, yet ten verses later the hero leaves this bride in the night, so the seven-birth bond in the epic marks the depth of love without securing its continuance.

gains.a: the phrase எழுமையும் இயைந்து is seen as the old wish for a husband across births, which the plot then strains
gains.b: the poem's prayer is set beside a story where love across births is granted and still does not stop separation, which shows why the woman must pray rather than assume

new_concepts.gloss: the wedding; the rite that makes a marriage
new_concepts.label_source: the label is the house word declared in earlier chapters; these verses use மணம் (1346) and மன்றல் (1346)

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: the verses name நரம்பின் இசை (1351) and the வீணை (1355)

source_issues: 1341, 1342, 1343, 1345, 1352-1356 and 1360 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build; the joins read correctly.
1348 lines 1-2 are compressed and the sense is not secure.
1353 has no named speaker and line 3 is obscure; the speaker is a guess.
